1.2.4.6-f102.accuracy_reason: Horace Sat. 1.3.127–28 mocks the Chrysippean claim that the wise man is a cobbler though he never made a shoe.

1.2.4.6-f103.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 83 reads 'sola pruinosis horret facundia pannis'.

1.2.4.6-f109.accuracy_reason: Porcius Licinus' verses in Suetonius' Vita Terenti read 'abit Graeciam in terram ultimam'.

1.2.4.6-f110.accuracy_reason: In Gnatho's speech at Eunuchus 2.2, 'video sentum squalidum aegrum, pannis annisque obsitum' comes several lines before 'hic ego illum contempsi prae me', so Burton does join separate lines.

1.2.4.6-f120.accuracy_reason: 'Genium defraudare' (Terence, Phormio 44, 'suom defrudans genium') is the idiom for stinting oneself, and the note explains it correctly.

1.2.4.6-f141.accuracy_reason: The Horace text is quoted correctly (Sat. 2.3.97–98). But Burton keeps both 'sapiens' and 'etiam'. He drops only the question and 'et', which turns the ironic exchange into a flat statement. He does not drop the words.

1.2.4.6-f19.accuracy_reason: Plutarch (Demosthenes 20) and Cicero (De Divinatione 2.118) report Demosthenes' gibe that the Pythia 'philippizes'.

1.2.4.6-f20.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.353, on Narcissus, reads 'multae cupiere puellae'.

1.2.4.6-f21.accuracy_reason: Petronius, Satyricon 137.9: 'Quisquis habet nummos, secura navigat aura… uxorem ducat Danaen'. The Danaë story is told correctly.

1.2.4.6-f26.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 5.135–137 reads 'ab ipsis / ilibus', and the lines imagine Virro fawning on Trebius if Trebius came into money.

1.2.4.6-f27.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.5.12–14 is Tiresias advising Ulysses on legacy-hunting, and first fruits were offered to the Lar.

1.2.4.6-f35.accuracy_reason: Machiavelli, Istorie fiorentine IV.16, gives Giovanni di Bicci's deathbed speech to Cosimo and Lorenzo. The note rightly hedges its reading of the sidenote.

1.2.4.6-f41.accuracy_reason: Persius 1.38–40 reads 'nunc non e manibus illis… nascentur violae?', a question asked after the dead poet has been praised.

1.2.4.6-f42.accuracy_reason: This is the first line of Horace, Satires 1.2, where flute-girls, quacks, beggars and mimae mourn Tigellius. Ambubaiae were Syrian flute-girls.

1.2.4.6-f43.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 37 says of Fortunata 'in caelum abiit' in the sense that she has risen in the world, and it has no 'recta'.

1.2.4.6-f5.accuracy_reason: Lucan 1.165–66 reads 'paupertas fugitur, totoque arcessitur orbe / quo gens quaeque perit'. So the subject of arcessitur is the luxury in the next line, and Burton does cut the line off.

1.2.4.6-f50.accuracy_reason: 'proiecta vilior alga' is Virgil, Eclogue 7.42. Horace, Satires 2.5.8 reads 'et genus et virtus nisi cum re vilior alga est', so the link to the 'Hor.' sidenote is apt and suitably hedged.

1.2.4.6-f51.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 13.141–42 sets 'gallinae filius albae' against 'nos viles pulli nati infelicibus ovis', as the note says.

1.2.4.6-f58.accuracy_reason: Being sent to the pistrinum is a stock threat to slaves in Plautus and Terence, and Sosia is a stock slave name. The rest of the note is a fair description of what Burton does.

1.2.4.6-f67.accuracy_reason: In Plutus (about lines 535–47), Chremylus lists what Poverty provides: lice, fleas, rags, a stone for a pillow, and so on.

1.2.4.6-f73.accuracy_reason: The full line is Juvenal 2.63, 'dat veniam corvis, vexat censura columbas', and the note gives its sense correctly.

1.2.4.6-f74.accuracy_reason: The note reads the dice throws correctly, and it is properly hedged ('appears to be') on whether the jingle was proverbial.

1.2.4.6-f75.accuracy_reason: The source is Georgics 4.83, 'ingentes animos angusto in pectore versant'. The note pairs the sidenote correctly with the main-text variant and identifies the augustas/angustas pun.

1.2.4.6-f77.accuracy_reason: It cites Georgics 4.83 correctly and links the line correctly to its paired sidenote.

1.2.4.6-f78.accuracy_reason: These verses are Porcius Licinus, quoted in Suetonius' Life of Terence.

1.2.4.6-f92.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 2.79–80 begins 'nec, si miserum Fortuna Sinonem / finxit, vanum etiam mendacemque improba finget', so dropping 'nec' does reverse the sense.

1.2.4.6-f95.accuracy_reason: Theognis 175–76 addresses Cyrnus ('Κύρνε') and speaks of the monster-filled sea and steep cliffs. Reading 'Cerne' as the vocative of Cyrnus is right, though it may be a variant spelling rather than a corruption.

1.2.4.6-f97.accuracy_reason: This is Alciato's emblem on poverty holding back great talents (one hand winged, the other holding a stone). In Alciato, 'Ut me pluma levat' comes before 'Ingenio poteram', so the note is right that Burton reverses them.
